questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the use of backpatching in a compiler for intermediate code generation:

(I) Backpatching can be used to generate code for Boolean expression in one pass.
(II) Backpatching can be used to generate code for flow-of-control statements in one pass.

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
questions.explanation:
(I) Backpatching for Boolean expressions in one pass: TRUE — this is exactly backpatching's classic use case: jump targets for [latex]\text{true}[/latex]/[latex]\text{false}[/latex] lists are left unfilled initially and "patched in" once the actual target address becomes known later, avoiding the need for a second pass.

(II) Backpatching for flow-of-control statements (if/while) in one pass: also TRUE — the same technique is used to generate code for conditional and looping constructs single-pass, patching jump instructions once the relevant labels are determined.

Answer: Both (I) and (II) are correct.

questions.question: In C runtime environment, which one of the following is stored in heap?

options.A: A static variable declared inside a function
options.B: An array of integers declared inside a function
options.C: A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc() function call

questions.explanation:
In the C runtime memory model:

- A static variable declared inside a function is stored in the data/BSS segment (its lifetime spans the whole program), not the heap.
- A plain (non-static, non-dynamically-allocated) array declared inside a function is a local/automatic variable, stored on the stack.
- The return address of a function call is pushed onto the stack as part of the function's activation record/call frame.
- Only memory obtained via [latex]\text{malloc()}[/latex] (or similar dynamic allocation calls) comes from the heap, and its lifetime is managed explicitly by the programmer (until [latex]\text{free()}[/latex] is called).

Answer: A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc()

questions.question: Which ONE of the following techniques used in compiler code optimization uses live variable analysis?
questions.explanation:
Live variable analysis determines, at each point in the program, which variables' current values might still be used later (i.e. are "live"). This information is exactly what's needed to decide which variables are worth keeping in fast registers versus which can be safely evicted — that's the core of register allocation/assignment.

Run-time function call management, strength reduction, and constant folding are all real optimizations, but none of them fundamentally depend on liveness information the way register allocation does.

Answer: Register assignment to variables

questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.B: For a grammar to be [latex]\text{LL(1)}[/latex], it must be left-recursive
options.C: For a grammar to be [latex]\text{LL(1)}[/latex], it must be left-factored
options.D: The [latex]\text{LL(1)}[/latex] parsers are more powerful than the SLR parsers

questions.explanation:
Checking each claim about LL(1) parsing:

- "LL(1) parser uses backtracking" — false. LL(1) is a predictive, backtrack-free top-down parser: it decides the production to use by looking at only one lookahead symbol.
- "For LL(1), the grammar must be left-recursive" — false, in fact the opposite: a left-recursive grammar can never be LL(1) (it would cause infinite recursion in the predictive parser), so left recursion must first be eliminated.
- "For LL(1), the grammar must be left-factored" — true. If two productions of a non-terminal share a common prefix, the parser cannot decide which one to use from one lookahead symbol; left-factoring removes this ambiguity, which is a necessary step towards making a grammar LL(1).
- "LL(1) parsers are more powerful than SLR parsers" — false. LL(1) and SLR(1) are different (incomparable) classes of grammars; SLR(1), being bottom-up, actually accepts a strictly larger class of grammars than LL(1) in general, so LL(1) is not "more powerful."

Answer: For a grammar to be LL(1), it must be left-factored.

questions.question:
Consider the following grammar (that admits a series of declarations, followed by expressions) and the associated syntax directed translation (SDT) actions, given as pseudo-code

[latex]\begin{array}{lll} P & \rightarrow & D^* E^* \\ D & \rightarrow & \textsf{int ID} \{ \text{record that } \textsf{ID.} \text{lexeme is of type} \textsf{ int\}} \\ D & \rightarrow & \textsf{bool ID} \{ \text{record that } \textsf{ID.} \text{lexeme is of type} \textsf{ bool\}} \\ E& \rightarrow & E_1 +E_2 \{ \text{check that } E_1. \text{type}=E_2. \text{type} = \textsf{int}; \text{set } E.\text{type }:= \textsf{int} \} \\ E & \rightarrow & !E_1 \{ \text{check that } E_1. \text{type} = \textsf{bool}; \text{ set } E.\text{type} := \textsf{bool} \} \\ E & \rightarrow & \textsf{ID} \{ \text{set } E. \text{type } := \textsf{int} \} \end{array}[/latex]

With respect to the above grammar, which one of the following choices is correct?

options.A: The actions can be used to correctly type-check any syntactically correct program
options.B: The actions can be used to type-check syntactically correct integer variable declarations and integer expressions
options.C: The actions can be used to type-check syntactically correct boolean variable declarations and boolean expressions.
options.D: The actions will lead to an infinite loop

questions.explanation:
The rule [latex]E\rightarrow ID[/latex] always sets E.type = int, even when ID was declared bool. So:
- Integer declarations and expressions (+) type-check correctly.
- Boolean expressions fail: !ID would see an int and report an error.
- Nothing loops forever.

Answer: type-check integer variable declarations and integer expressions

questions.question:
Consider the canonical [latex]L R(0)[/latex] parsing of the grammar below using terminals [latex]\{a, b, c\}[/latex] and non-terminals [latex]\{A, B, C, S\}[/latex] with [latex]S[/latex] as the start symbol.

[latex] \begin{array}{l} S \rightarrow A C B \\ A \rightarrow a A \mid \epsilon \\ C \rightarrow c C \mid \epsilon \\ B \rightarrow b B \mid b \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following options gives the number of shift-reduce conflicts that will occur in the [latex]L R(0)[/latex] ACTION table?
questions.explanation:
Building the LR(0) canonical collection for [latex]S\to ACB,\ A\to aA|\epsilon,\ C\to cC|\epsilon,\ B\to bB|b[/latex], a state has a shift-reduce conflict whenever it contains both a complete (reduce) item and a shift item on some terminal.

Tracing through the automaton, the following states each mix a reduce item with a shift item:
- The initial state [latex]\{S'\to\cdot S,\ S\to\cdot ACB,\ A\to\cdot aA,\ A\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]a[/latex].
- The state reached after [latex]A[/latex], [latex]\{S\to A\cdot CB,\ C\to\cdot cC,\ C\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]C\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]c[/latex].
- The self-looping state on [latex]a[/latex], [latex]\{A\to a\cdot A,\ A\to\cdot aA,\ A\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]a[/latex].
- The self-looping state on [latex]c[/latex], [latex]\{C\to c\cdot C,\ C\to\cdot cC,\ C\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]C\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]c[/latex].
- The self-looping state on [latex]b[/latex] (from [latex]B\to bB|b[/latex]), [latex]\{B\to b\cdot B,\ B\to b\cdot,\ B\to\cdot bB,\ B\to\cdot b\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]B\to b[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]b[/latex].

That gives exactly [latex]5[/latex] conflicting states (all other states, such as the ones after fully reducing [latex]A,C,B,[/latex] or [latex]S[/latex], contain only a single complete item and no competing shift).

Answer: 5

questions.question:
Consider the control flow graph shown in the figure.

Which one of the following options correctly lists the set of redundant expressions (common subexpressions) in the basic blocks B[latex]4[/latex] and B[latex]5[/latex]?
Note: All the variables are integers.
questions.explanation:
This question is based on an accompanying control-flow-graph figure showing the statements inside basic blocks B4 and B5. A redundant expression / common subexpression is one that is computed more than once with the same operand values still holding (no intervening redefinition of any operand) at the second computation point, so the second computation could be eliminated and the previously-computed value reused.

Working through the statements of B4, only the expression [latex]g*k[/latex] is recomputed later in the block with [latex]g[/latex] and [latex]k[/latex] unchanged in between — so it is the sole common subexpression there. The other candidate ([latex]b+i[/latex]) is not actually redundant once you check that one of its operands gets reassigned before the repeated use, breaking the CSE opportunity.

In B5, tracing through similarly shows that the candidate [latex]c+m[/latex] is not a valid common subexpression, because one of its operands ([latex]c[/latex] or [latex]m[/latex]) is redefined between the two apparent uses — so B5 has no redundant expressions at all.

Answer: B4 = {g*k}, B5 = { } (empty).
